title: Placaeus: fallen man is free from three necessities but has lost the power not to sin
source_text: XXV. Quibus consentanea sunt quae docet Josue Placeus tractatu de libero hominis arbitrio capite quarto, quod est de Libero Hominis arbitrio in statu peccati. Est, inquit, in posteris Adami facultas arbitrandi & volendi libera a triplici necessitate coactionis, scilicet, qualem pati potest corpus nostrum, determinationis a materia, maxime qualis cernitur in lapidibus & stipitibus, & sensus qualis competit brutis animantibus, cujus ratione homo est subjectum δεκτικὸν vel vitii, vel virtutis, ac Dei legi obnoxius. Quibus postea subjungit, Quam igitur arbitrii libertatem amisit Adamus? Amisit facultatem absolutam non peccandi sitam in justitia originali, quae posita est partim in naturali facultatum moralium integritate, perfectione, rectitudine absque ullo vitio, morbo, ἀταξίᾳ, errore, partim in appetitu veri finis ultimi, & ex illo appetitu enatis habitibus bene vivendi inchoatis, qui secundum naturae ordinem paulatim crevissent ad summum usque perfectionis gradum. In hujus libertatis locum successit servitus peccati sita in depravatione atque obliquitate facultatum moralium, praesertim voluntatis: ea vero depravatio consistit in aversione a vero fine ultimo, & conversione ad finem ultimum falso apparentem. Ex quo sequitur, cum quicquid appetitur sit aut finis ultimus, aut medium ad illud, nihil sani reliquum esse factum in facultatibus nostris moralibus. Neque id solum, sed quamdiu sic affecti sumus, fieri non posse quin peccemus.
pass_a_gloss: XXV. With which agree the things which Josué de la Place teaches in the treatise on the free choice of man in chapter four, which is on the Free choice of Man in the state of sin. There is, he says, in the posterity of Adam a faculty of judging and willing free from a threefold necessity, of coaction, namely, such as our body can suffer, of determination by matter, most of all such as is seen in stones and stocks, and of sense such as belongs to brute animals, by reason of which man is a subject receptive either of vice, or of virtue, and liable to the law of God. To which he afterwards subjoins, What freedom of choice then did Adam lose? He lost the absolute faculty of not sinning placed in original righteousness, which was placed partly in the natural integrity of the moral faculties, perfection, rectitude without any vice, disease, disorder, error, partly in the appetite for the true last end, and in the habits of living well begun, born from that appetite, which according to the order of nature would have grown little by little up to the highest degree of perfection. In the place of this freedom succeeded the servitude of sin placed in the depravation and obliquity of the moral faculties, especially the will: and that depravation consists in aversion from the true last end, and conversion to a falsely apparent last end. From which it follows, since whatever is desired is either the last end, or a means to it, that nothing sound is left remaining in our moral faculties. And not that only, but that as long as we are so affected, it cannot be but that we sin.
pass_b_english: This agrees with what Josué de la Place teaches in his treatise on man's free choice, chapter 4, which deals with man's free choice in the state of sin. 'In Adam's descendants,' he says, 'there is a faculty of judging and willing that is free from a threefold necessity: from compulsion, such as our body can suffer; from determination by matter, chiefly as seen in stones and logs; and from sense, as belongs to brute animals. Because of this faculty man is a subject capable of either vice or virtue, and answerable to God's law.'

He then adds: 'What freedom of choice, then, did Adam lose? He lost the absolute power of not sinning that lay in original righteousness. This lay partly in the natural integrity of the moral faculties, their perfection and rectitude, free of any vice, disease, disorder or error; partly in the desire for the true last end and in the habits of good living that sprang from that desire, which by the order of nature would have grown little by little to the highest degree of perfection.

In place of this freedom came the bondage of sin, which lies in the corruption and crookedness of the moral faculties, especially the will. That corruption consists in turning away from the true last end and turning toward a last end that only falsely appears to be one.

Since whatever is desired is either the last end or a means to it, it follows that nothing sound is left in our moral faculties. And more than that: as long as we are in that condition, we cannot help sinning.'

lemmas.gloss: free from a threefold necessity, of coaction
He lost the absolute faculty of not sinning
it cannot be but that we sin

choices.why: The will's slavery to sin, opposed to the freedom lost in the fall; 'bondage' keeps the Augustinian sense.
